title: Bank stocks: how to analyze banks — P/B, ROE and rates
description: How to analyze bank stocks: P/B, ROE, net interest income, the credit loss cycle and capital adequacy — the method step by step, with sources.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Bank stocks are shares in companies whose raw material is money itself. A bank takes in deposits and market funding at one rate, lends the same money out at a higher one — and the difference, net interest income, is the heart of the business. The analysis therefore looks different from a manufacturer's: leverage is not a risk metric but the business model itself, the P/E says less than the P/B, and the most important single number is return on equity — ROE.

This guide walks through the mechanics: the mirror-image balance sheet, P/B and ROE, the rate and credit loss cycles, capital adequacy — and a five-step checklist. All examples are worked calculations and real key ratios from our company universe — education in method, never guidance about individual stocks.

## The bank's balance sheet — mirror image of everyone else's

An ordinary company collects assets — factories, inventory, receivables — financed by equity and debt. The bank starts at the other end: the assets are the lending itself — mortgages, corporate credit, bonds — financed mostly with other people's money — deposits and market funding. Equity is a thin cushion at the bottom — a few percent of the balance sheet. The basics are in [the balance sheet — the company's map](/kurser/bk-01-balansrakningen) and [how to read a balance sheet in 15 minutes](/blogg/sa-laser-du-en-balansrakning-pa-15-minuter).

The consequence: lending is the bank's business, not its risk per se. A manufacturer borrowing five times its equity is aggressively leveraged; a bank at the same ratio is normally financed. The risk metrics therefore switch sides — [the debt-to-equity ratio](/blogg/vad-ar-skuldsattningsgrad) says nothing about a bank, and capital adequacy steps in instead (below). Earnings switch sides too: governed by rates and credit losses, not a product margin.

## Key ratios for bank stocks — P/B and ROE at the center

For bank stocks the P/B ratio is the headline multiple: share price divided by equity per share. The logic: a bank's assets and liabilities are essentially money, continuously valued at market, so equity is a reasonable starting point for value — the price against it shows how the market judges the bank's ability to earn on it. [P/B — when book value compares fairly](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt) goes through the measure in depth.

ROE — result divided by equity — is the engine, and the relationship is pure arithmetic: P/E = P/B ÷ ROE. Worked example from the universe: Swedbank with P/B 2.07 and ROE 15.0 percent gives 2.07 ÷ 0.150 ≈ 13.8 — exactly the bank's P/E in the same data. The four large Swedish banks in the universe (data collected 2026-09-03, verified 2026-09-15):

- Swedbank: ROE 15.0 percent, P/B 2.1, P/E 13.8
- Nordea: ROE 15.3 percent, P/E 13.0 (P/B missing in the source data — omitted, not guessed)
- SEB: ROE 14.1 percent, P/B 1.9, P/E 14.4
- Handelsbanken: ROE 12.8 percent, P/B 1.6, P/E 12.4

A P/B above 1 means the market expects an ROE above the required return — equity compounding faster than the cost of capital. A P/B below 1 means the opposite: the market doubts the booked equity can earn back its value. P/B and ROE are question and answer; neither stands alone. Calculate ROE yourself: [how to calculate ROE](/blogg/hur-raknar-man-roe).

## The interest rate — the bank's business cycle

Net interest income — lending out at a higher rate than the bank borrows in — is the largest income item and the most rate-sensitive. The mechanics of a hike: loan pricing adjusts with the policy rate while deposit rates lag — the margin widens; in a cut it compresses again unless volumes grow. The 2021–2025 cycle illustrates it: the Riksbank raised the policy rate from zero to four percent in under two years, then stepped down. The universe's data shows it directly: three of four major banks have falling net margins from the 2023 peak — Handelsbanken from 46.8 to 41.8 percent, SEB from 47.5 to 40.4 and Nordea from 42.0 to 41.2 — while Swedbank is the exception (46.7 versus 47.7 percent).

The tools are in [interest — the price of money](/kurser/km-054-ranta), [central banks](/kurser/km-056-centralbanker) and [interest rate risk — duration](/kurser/rk-08-ranterisk).

## Credit losses — the risk that cycles

The second engine is fee income — payments, advisory, asset management, brokerage — offset by credit losses: loans not paid back. Credit losses are the cycle's dark mirror: near zero in the upswing, capital-eaters in the downturn. The lesson is free in Swedish history: in the 1990s crisis the property market cracked, credit losses tore balance sheets apart, and Nordbanken and Gota ended up in state ownership with support — the Swedish supervision model was built afterwards. The risk has modern shapes: the money laundering case around Swedbank in 2019 showed compliance risk hitting hard — dug into in [Case: Swedbank](/kurser/pc-03-case-swedbank).

The credit loss level is reported as a share of lending; compare it through a whole cycle, not a single peak year — near-zero losses one year only say the cycle was kind.

## Capital adequacy — the rules that protect and constrain

Because the bank is built on other people's money, a regulatory frame surrounds it. Basel III requires equity of at least a set share of risk-weighted assets — a base ratio plus buffers; in Sweden Finansinspektionen, the financial supervisor, sets the requirements, the largest banks also paying a systemic risk buffer. Swedish majors historically hold good margins above the minimum.

The rules play a double role. They protect: a well-filled capital buffer makes the credit loss cycle survivable. They constrain: every extra krona of capital lowers ROE, because the denominator grows. The capital adequacy ratio is the bank's counterpart to solidity — [solidity and interest coverage ratio](/kurser/st-01-soliditet-och-rantetackning) explains the classical variant — and a bank with high adequacy and high ROE at once combines two things that usually pull apart.

## How to analyze bank stocks — a five-step checklist

1. **The share of net interest income.** How much of the revenue is net interest income? A large fee share means less rate sensitivity.
2. **ROE through the cycle.** Look at five years, not one. Sustainable ROE is the engine behind P/B — short-term peaks are not.
3. **P/B against ROE and history.** Set P/B against the bank's own five-year history and comparable banks; let P/E = P/B ÷ ROE be the cross-check.
4. **The credit losses.** Level through the cycle, the bank's forecast, the exposure's orientation — mortgages, corporate credit and foreign lending are different risk worlds.
5. **Capital and dividends.** Capital adequacy with margin, a payout ratio leaving capital to grow with; bank dividends are often valued with dividend models — [the Dividend Discount Model](/kurser/vm-06-dividend-discount-model-ddm) shows the method.

## Three mistakes worth clearing up

- **The debt-to-equity ratio of a bank.** Meaningless — banks are by construction built on borrowed money. The meaningful measure is the capital adequacy ratio.
- **One rate year is not a trend.** The 2023 margins were a rate peak, not a new normal. Value net interest income through a whole rate cycle.
- **P/B without ROE.** A low P/B can be cheap equity — or equity that never earns its cost. The difference lies entirely in ROE and its sustainability.

## The summary

- The bank's raw material is money: the balance sheet is the business, equity a thin cushion under other people's money.
- P/B and ROE are the headline measures, and P/E = P/B ÷ ROE binds them together. In the universe: ROE 12.8–15.3 percent and P/E 12.4–14.4 for the four large Swedish banks.
- Net interest income swings with the policy rate — three of four major banks show falling net margins after the 2023 peak.
- Credit losses cycle and are the biggest single risk; capital adequacy rules are both protection and ceiling on ROE.

Where the track continues: [the Bank Sector](/kurser/km-040-banksektorn) covers the sector's mechanics, [the sector medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) show how banks stand against other sectors, and the whole workflow is in [the complete guide to Swedish equity analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).
